Factors Influencing the Utilisation of High-Performance 
Computing (HPC) Systems in Higher Education Institutions 
Authors: 
Reginald Mulalo Ndwamai (reginaldmulalo@outlook.com, ORCID: 0000-0002-3341-9540) 
Department of Human Resource Management and Labour Relations, University of Venda, 
Thohoyandou, South Africa 
Hlanganipai Ngirande (hlanganipai@gmail.com, ORCID: 0000-0003-2604-2156) 
Department of Human Resource Management and Labour Relations, University of Venda, 
Thohoyandou, South Africa 
This paper is part of the 1st Human Resource Management International Conference (HRMIC) on 
“Innovative Human Resource Strategies for Workforce Resilience and Sustainable Development.” The 
conference was hosted by the University of Venda, South Africa, and Moi University, Kenya, in Eldoret, 
Kenya, in June 2025. Wohllebe & Ross is honored to have been selected to publish the conference 
proceedings as a special issue of the International Journal of Applied Research in Business and 
Management (ISSN 2700-8983). 
Abstract: 
Understanding how organisational support, perceived ease of use, and perceived usefulness influence 
the actual use of a High-Performance Computing (HPC) system sheds light on its adoption within a 
higher education institution. A quantitative approach with a descriptive design was employed, surveying 
218 respondents, including Master's and PhD students and academic staff, using stratified and simple 
random sampling techniques. Data were collected through online self-administered questionnaires and 
analysed using SPSS version 29.0. The findings revealed strong positive correlations between 
organisational support, perceived ease of use, perceived usefulness, and actual use of the HPC system, 
supporting prior research on technology adoption (Davis, 1989; Venkatesh et al., 2003). A moderate 
positive correlation was found between organisational support and perceived ease of use and perceived 
usefulness. This suggests that users who feel supported by their institution are more likely to find the 
system easy to use and valuable. Furthermore, a moderate positive correlation was found between 
perceived ease of use and perceived usefulness, as well as between perceived ease of use and actual 
use, indicating that users who find the system simple to use are more likely to adopt it. Additionally, there 
was a moderate positive correlation between perceived usefulness and actual use, highlighting that 
users engage more with the system when they recognise its benefits. In conclusion, organisational 
support and user perceptions are key to successfully implementing and using new technologies.

Introduction and Background 
In the contemporary digital landscape of academia, High-Performance Computing (HPC) has emerged 
as a fundamental component of higher education, particularly for institutions aiming to foster innovative 
research and cultivate the next generation of scientists and innovators. HPC systems empower students 
and faculty to manage extensive datasets, conduct simulations, and address intricate problems that 
would be unfeasible with conventional computing resources. For postgraduate students and researchers 
engaged in data-intensive disciplines, HPC is not merely advantageous; it is essential (Hebert et al., 
2024). 
Globally, universities are increasingly acknowledging the significance of High-Performance Computing 
(HPC) in fostering academic innovation and are making substantial investments in its infrastructure. For 
instance, state universities in Zimbabwe have demonstrated a rising interest in HPC to enhance their 
advanced teaching and research objectives (Mutunhu, Nyathi & Dube, 2021). Likewise, institutions in 
the United States are investigating methods to incorporate HPC into undergraduate curricula, 
recognising both advancements and ongoing challenges in this endeavour (Hebert et al., 2024).  
The underlying message is evident: although the technology is accessible, effectively engaging users 
remains a complex issue. A significant obstacle to the adoption of HPC is not the technology itself, but 
rather the manner in which it is introduced, supported, and perceived. Even when institutions offer 
access to robust computing resources, many users lack the confidence, motivation, or practical skills 
necessary for effective utilisation (Al-Jody, Aagela & Holmes, 2021). This challenge is particularly 
pronounced in environments where training is sporadic or support systems are inadequately developed. 
Consequently, those who would benefit the most—postgraduate students and early-career 
researchers—often find themselves underutilising these valuable tools. 
Statement of the Problem 
High-Performance Computing (HPC) systems have increasingly become available in higher education 
institutions globally, with the potential to transform teaching, learning, and research through advanced 
data processing and modeling capabilities. However, despite substantial investments in HPC 
infrastructure, numerous institutions are not achieving the expected benefits, primarily due to the limited 
engagement of the very individuals these systems are designed to assist (Mutunhu, Nyathi & Dube, 
2021). Often, postgraduate students and academic staff continue to depend on conventional computing 
methods, resulting in HPC resources being underutilised or completely overlooked.  
This widening disparity between technological availability and user participation underscores a more 
profound issue: the challenge extends beyond mere access to technology; it encompasses perceptions, 
support, and adoption within institutional contexts. As noted by Hebert et al. (2024), even when

Aim of this Paper 
This paper sought to investigate the influence of perceived ease of use, perceived usefulness, and 
organisational support on the actual use of a High-Performance Computing (HPC) system in a higher 
education institution. 
Research Objectives 
• 
To assess the relationship between perceived ease of use and the actual use of the HPC 
system. 
• 
To evaluate the influence of perceived usefulness on the actual use of the HPC system. 
• 
To examine the role of organisational support in influencing perceived ease of use and 
perceived usefulness. 
• 
To determine how organisational support affects the actual use of the HPC system. 
Research Hypotheses 
H1: There was a positive relationship between perceived ease of use and the actual use of the HPC 
system. 
H2: There was a positive relationship between perceived usefulness and the actual use of the HPC 
system. 
H3: Organisational support positively influenced perceived ease of use and perceived usefulness of the 
HPC system. 
H4: Organisational support positively influenced the actual use of the HPC system. 
Significance of this Paper 
Practical Significance 
This paper offers real, hands-on value for universities and colleges trying to get the most out of their 
investment in High-Performance Computing (HPC) systems. While institutions often spend heavily on 
acquiring the latest HPC infrastructure, it’s clear that providing the technology alone is not enough. What 
really matters is whether people, especially postgraduate students and academic staff, are using these 
systems effectively. By highlighting the key factors that influence actual use, such as perceived ease of 
use, perceived usefulness, and the level of organisational support, this research points to practical ways

institutions can bridge the gap between access and adoption. For instance, the findings can help guide 
better-designed training programs, more responsive user support services, and system interfaces that 
feel more intuitive and approachable to everyday users. 
On a broader level, this paper helps institutions think more strategically about how they roll out and 
support complex technologies like HPC. Rather than treating the problem as a purely technical one, the 
research encourages decision-makers to consider the human side of adoption. This includes building a 
culture of support, investing in user education, and tailoring communication about the benefits of HPC 
to different academic roles and disciplines. When people understand how a system can help them in 
their specific research or teaching context—and when they feel supported using it—they’re far more 
likely to embrace it. These practical takeaways can lead to more effective use of HPC systems and, 
ultimately, stronger research output and innovation. 
Theoretical Significance  
In addition to its practical implications, this research contributes a novel perspective to our 
comprehension of technology adoption within academic environments. It expands upon the established 
Technology Acceptance Model (TAM), which posits that individuals' readiness to embrace new 
technology is primarily influenced by their perceptions of its utility and ease of use. However, this study 
advances the discourse by incorporating organisational support as a significant factor that affects these 
fundamental beliefs. This implies that user perceptions of the system are not the sole determinants; 
instead, the extent to which they feel supported by their institution, through resources, encouragement, 
and guidance, also plays a vital role in their engagement with the technology.  
By integrating this aspect into TAM, the research enhances the theoretical framework, making it more 
applicable to the complexities of university life. Academic settings are multifaceted, characterized by 
diverse user requirements, competing priorities, and often constrained time. This study recognises the 
importance of context and illustrates how institutional culture and support mechanisms are pivotal in 
influencing technology adoption. Consequently, it offers a more comprehensive framework that aids 
scholars, IT professionals, and educational researchers in understanding not only the likelihood of 
individuals utilizing high-performance computing systems but also the underlying reasons for their 
choices. This paves the way for new avenues of inquiry and theoretical development in the realm of 
educational technology. 
Theoretical Framework (Technology Acceptance Model) 
The exploration of the factors influencing the adoption or rejection of new technologies has been a 
pivotal focus within the field of information systems research. The Technology Acceptance Model (TAM), 
introduced by Davis in 1989, provides a straightforward and pragmatic framework: individuals are more

inclined to utilise a technology if they perceive it as beneficial to their performance (perceived 
usefulness) and if they believe it is user-friendly (perceived ease of use). These perceptions significantly 
shape their attitudes towards the technology, which subsequently affects their actual usage behavior. 
Over the years, scholars have acknowledged that TAM does not function in isolation.  
Elements such as organisational culture, support, training, and peer influence can all impact how users 
develop these perceptions. Venkatesh et al. (2003) broadened the scope of TAM to incorporate these 
contextual factors, underscoring the necessity of considering broader organisational and social 
dynamics in adoption frameworks. In their research, organizational support was identified as a 
fundamental variable affecting both perceived ease of use and perceived usefulness. This finding is 
consistent with the work of Tao et al. (2020), who assert that institutional support—encompassing 
training, access, and leadership endorsement—plays a vital role in shaping user engagement with 
technology.  
The findings of this study affirm that organisational support is not merely advantageous; it is crucial. 
Participants who perceived institutional support were more likely to regard the HPC system as both 
useful and easy to use, which significantly predicted their actual engagement with the system. This 
aligns with the conclusions drawn by Legris, Ingham, and Collerette (2003), who demonstrated that 
support mechanisms considerably enhance the predictive validity of TAM in practical environments. 
Likewise, Tetik et al. (2024) highlight that when users receive ongoing guidance and recognise that their 
institution values the system, their confidence and readiness to adopt it are markedly increased.  
Therefore, enhances the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) by incorporating organisational support, 
thereby not only applying the model but also broadening its scope. This approach contributes to a deeper 
and more nuanced comprehension of the interactions between academic personnel and postgraduate 
students with intricate systems such as High-Performance Computing (HPC). Furthermore, it 
corroborates the findings of previous scholars who have noted that the successful adoption of 
technology transcends the mere functionality of the tool; it is significantly influenced by the contextual 
environment in which users operate (Tao et al., 2020; Tetik et al., 2024; Legris et al., 2003; Venkatesh 
et al., 2003). 
Conceptualisation and Interaction 
Perceived ease of use 
The concept of perceived ease of use pertains to the degree to which users find the HPC system 
straightforward and uncomplicated during their interactions, which is crucial in influencing their decision 
to adopt and persist in utilising the technology (Richmond & Wasserman, 2018). For numerous academic 
users—particularly those lacking a background in computational sciences—the initial encounter with

HPC systems may evoke feelings of complexity and technical difficulty (Alnasir et al., 2021). This 
perception can hinder engagement, especially in disciplines such as life sciences, where users' technical 
skills can vary significantly (Richmond & Wasserman, 2018). Nevertheless, when the system is regarded 
as intuitive and user-friendly, individuals are more inclined to engage with it, thereby enhancing the 
probability of consistent usage (Kocot et al., 2023).  
The findings indicate that participants who perceived the HPC platform as user-friendly exhibited 
markedly higher levels of engagement, underscoring the pivotal role of perceived ease of use in shaping 
adoption trends (Alnasir et al., 2021). The necessity of minimising technical obstacles is supported by 
research demonstrating that well-designed and accessible user interfaces can diminish psychological 
barriers, promoting wider adoption among both novice and seasoned users (Richmond & Wasserman, 
2018; Kocot et al., 2023). Furthermore, the provision of precise instructions, comprehensive 
documentation, and technical support can significantly enhance perceptions of usability, thereby 
facilitating more substantial interactions with HPC resources (Alnasir et al., 2021). 
Perceived usefulness 
Perceived usefulness connects to the extent to which users believe that the high-performance 
computing (HPC) system enhances their productivity, especially regarding academic or research 
outcomes (Apon et al., 2014). This belief often serves as a significant driver for continued usage; when 
users acknowledge that the system facilitates more efficient task execution or allows them to achieve 
results that would otherwise be challenging, their dedication to utilising it increases (Kocot et al., 2023). 
In the present study, participants who recognised distinct research benefits—such as accelerated data 
processing and enhanced analytical capabilities—exhibited markedly higher engagement with the HPC 
system (Alnasir et al., 2021).  
These results corroborate previous research indicating that when HPC tools are well-aligned with 
academic objectives, users are more inclined to integrate them into their workflows (Apon et al., 2014). 
For example, numerous users indicated that high-performance computing enabled them to perform 
simulations and handle data sets that would be impractical with traditional systems, thereby reinforcing 
the system's significance (Kocot et al., 2023). This aligns with the findings of Richmond and Wasserman 
(2018), which suggest that when researchers can clearly identify how HPC resources enhance their 
scientific productivity, the frequency of usage increases.  
Organisational support 
Even the most advanced system will fall flat without the right kind of organisational support. 
Organisational support includes everything from training and technical assistance to making sure there 
are enough resources (like help desks or tutorials) and creating a culture that encourages usage. This

paper found that when users felt their institution was behind them, providing support, encouragement, 
and clear guidance, they were more likely to engage with the HPC system meaningfully. It is not just 
about offering the technology; it’s about creating an environment where users feel empowered to explore 
and adopt it. As Kocot et al. (2023) point out, support structures play a critical role in helping users adapt 
to and manage the complex nature of HPC systems, especially when energy consumption and 
scheduling become user concerns. 
In practice, this means institutions need to go beyond hardware investment—they need to invest in 
people. That includes ongoing training, technical staff who understand both the systems and the users’ 
academic goals, and leadership that champions innovation. 
Actual use of the HPC system 
Finally, actual use reflects what users are doing on the ground: how often and how extensively they are 
interacting with the HPC system. It’s the most concrete outcome, shaped by the interplay of ease of use, 
usefulness, and organisational support. This paper found strong links between the other three factors 
and actual system usage. Those who found the HPC system easy to use, useful, and supported by their 
institutions were far more likely to integrate it into their academic routines. They weren’t just logging in—
they were using it meaningfully for research simulations, data analysis, and large-scale computing tasks. 
Therefore, this is in line with findings from Alnasir and Koka (2019), who highlighted how training and 
technical empowerment drive actual engagement with HPC platforms in research contexts.  
Relationship Amongst the Factors 
In the context of implementing high-performance computing (HPC) systems within academic institutions, 
the mere presence of appropriate technology is seldom sufficient. The actual utilisation of these 
advanced tools by students and faculty is significantly affected by their sense of support and 
preparedness. This paper indicates that organisational support—encompassing aspects such as 
training, technical assistance, and motivation—plays a crucial role in shaping users' perceptions of the 
system's usability and utility. These perceptions, in turn, directly influence the frequency and 
effectiveness of engagement with the HPC system. 
When individuals perceive that their institution provides adequate support through responsive technical 
assistance, conducting training sessions, or ensuring the availability of necessary resources, they are 
more inclined to view the system as user-friendly. This is logical; when faced with a complicated system, 
the assurance of available help alleviates anxiety. Research conducted by Richmond and Wasserman 
(2018) indicates that organised support can enable users, particularly those lacking technical expertise, 
to engage with high-performance computing tools they might typically shy away from.

Organisational support not only facilitates the usability of systems but also enhances users' recognition 
of their value. When high-performance computing (HPC) platforms are actively endorsed as vital for 
research or academic pursuits, both students and faculty are more inclined to regard them as essential 
for achieving their objectives. Apon et al. (2014) noted that academic institutions with strong HPC 
infrastructure often experience increased research productivity, primarily because users acknowledge 
and trust the advantages provided by the system.  
Furthermore, the research indicated that organisational support not only influences perceptions but can 
also directly affect actual usage. Even prior to fully understanding the system's utility or user-friendliness, 
the mere existence of visible and consistent institutional support can encourage users to interact with 
the system more regularly. This aligns with the findings of Alnasir et al. (2021), who emphasized that 
effective onboarding and institutional motivation can accelerate the adoption of HPC among 
researchers. Overall, this interplay—where organisational support affects both perceptions and actual 
behavior—reflects the insights of various extended versions of the Technology Acceptance Model 
(TAM). Adoption is not driven by a singular factor but rather by a series of influences, where support 
fosters positive perceptions that subsequently encourage sustained usage. 
Methodology 
A quantitative research design was employed using a descriptive approach. The study involved 218 
respondents from a higher education institution, comprising Master's and PhD students as well as 
academic staff. Stratified and simple random sampling techniques ensured representativeness across 
academic levels and departments. Data were collected using an online self-administered questionnaire. 
Responses were analysed using SPSS version 29.0 to assess relationships among variables using 
correlation and regression analyses. 
Results 
According to Pallant (2019), Cronbach's Alpha values can be interpreted as follows: an alpha value 
greater than 0.9 is considered excellent, indicating high internal consistency. Values between 0.8 and 
0.9 are deemed good, suggesting reliable measures. A value ranging from 0.7 to 0.8 is acceptable, 
demonstrating adequate reliability. If the value falls between 0.6 and 0.7, it is questionable, implying 
some concerns with internal consistency. Values between 0.5 and 0.6 are considered poor, while 
anything below 0.5 is deemed unacceptable, indicating poor reliability of the scale.

Discussion 
This paper aimed to explore the factors that influence the utilisation of High-Performance Computing 
(HPC) systems within a university setting. Central to this investigation was a fundamental yet significant 
question: what motivates certain postgraduate students and academic staff to engage with HPC systems 
actively? In contrast, others remain reluctant, despite the availability of such technology. The findings 
provide compelling evidence that the mere presence of tools is insufficient; rather, the effectiveness of 
these tools in the academic experience is contingent upon the support, perception, and practical 
applicability they offer. One of the most significant conclusions drawn from the study was the critical role 
of institutional support.  
With a Cronbach’s Alpha of 0.846, the internal consistency of this factor was robust, suggesting that 
participants regarded it as a trustworthy element. This observation corroborates the findings of 
Richmond and Wasserman (2018), who noted that individuals are significantly more inclined to utilise 
complex systems like HPC when they perceive institutional backing in the form of training, technical 
assistance, and motivation. Furthermore, Alnasir (2021) emphasized that support frameworks are 
essential for closing the gap between technical capabilities and user preparedness in academic 
contexts. Without adequate guidance, even the most advanced systems risk remaining underutilized. 
Similarly, the perceived ease of use was a significant factor. Scoring 0.846 on the reliability scale, this 
aspect was found to have a considerable impact on user engagement with the HPC system. For 
numerous participants, particularly those lacking a computer science background, perceiving the system 
as user-friendly alleviated anxiety and enhanced confidence. As Kocot, Czarnul and Proficz (2023) 
highlighted in their examination of energy-aware scheduling in HPC, the design and usability of the 
system are as vital as its computational capabilities. When users find the system accessible, they are 
more inclined to utilize it consistently. Richmond and Wasserman (2018) reinforced this notion, indicating 
that clear instructions and intuitive interfaces can significantly elevate user adoption rates. 
Furthermore, perceived usefulness, which recorded a slightly lower yet robust Cronbach's Alpha of 
0.792, addresses the inquiry: "Is this system a valuable investment of my time?" The findings 
unequivocally indicated that when users perceive the HPC system as a means to enhance their 
productivity, whether through expedited simulations, improved research outcomes, or more 
comprehensive data analysis, they are considerably more likely to engage with it. Apon, Ngo, Payne 
and Wilson (2014) corroborate this, asserting that institutions equipped with robust HPC resources 
frequently experience heightened academic productivity and innovation, especially in research-focused 
fields.

Remarkably, the interplay of three critical factors—support, user-friendliness, and perceived utility—
significantly influenced the actual utilisation of the HPC system, achieving a score of 0.809. This score 
suggests that these constructs were not merely theoretical; they manifested in observable behaviours. 
Participants who experienced adequate support, found the system user-friendly, and recognized its 
practical advantages were the most engaged with the technology. These findings reinforce the extended 
Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) proposed by Venkatesh et al. (2003), which acknowledges both 
direct and indirect influences on user behavior.  
Additionally, Tao et al. (2020) discovered that when organisational and usability factors are in harmony, 
the use of technology seamlessly integrates into the workflow rather than becoming a hindrance. The 
results underscore the necessity of a comprehensive strategy. It is insufficient for institutions to 
implement costly HPC systems and expect user engagement merely. They must also commit to 
continuous user training, highlight the system's practical advantages, and provide readily available 
technical support. As Tetik et al. (2024) pointed out in their research on health information systems, user 
adoption hinges as much on experience and perception as it does on functionality. In conclusion, this 
paper validates a long-held belief in academic technology circles: support, ease of use, and perceived 
value are essential for realising the full potential of HPC systems in higher education.  
Conclusion 
This paper fundamentally emphasizes that the adoption of technology transcends mere machinery; it 
fundamentally involves human factors. In settings where High-Performance Computing (HPC) systems 
are abundantly available, their effective utilisation is often contingent upon users' perceptions and the 
level of institutional support they receive. The findings indicate that when academic personnel and 
postgraduate students feel adequately supported, perceive the systems as user-friendly, and recognise 
their intrinsic value, they are significantly more inclined to incorporate HPC into their routine research 
and academic activities. 
By employing the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) as a foundational framework and enhancing it 
with the aspect of organisational support, this paper provides a more comprehensive understanding of 
the factors influencing technology utilisation in higher education. It underscores that while ease of use 
and perceived usefulness remain critical, they do not exist in isolation. Institutional support is pivotal in 
shaping these perceptions and the subsequent behaviours that ensue. 
For universities that are making substantial investments in advanced technologies such as HPC, the 
implications are evident: achieving success extends beyond mere installation. Continuous training, 
accessible technical assistance, and a nurturing culture are equally vital as the technologies themselves. 
This paper not only corroborates existing technology adoption models but also modifies them to align

Limitation 
A significant drawback is its sole dependence on a quantitative methodology. Although this approach 
facilitated the assessment of trends, correlations, and statistical validity, it failed to encompass the 
richness of participants' individual experiences, motivations, or difficulties encountered while utilising the 
HPC system. Quantitative data inherently tends to simplify user feedback into numerical trends, 
potentially neglecting the intricate insights that qualitative data, like interviews or focus groups, could 
reveal. Consequently, this paper overlooked critical contextual factors that shape user behavior and 
perceptions regarding HPC utilisation. 
Recommendation 
To enhance the existing findings, subsequent investigations should consider implementing a mixed-
methods strategy that integrates both quantitative and qualitative data. This approach would enable 
researchers to not only identify patterns and correlations but also to delve into the underlying factors 
influencing user perceptions and behaviours. For example, conducting semi-structured interviews with 
users could reveal specific obstacles to usability or clarify the types of organisational support that are 
most beneficial. Furthermore, broadening the scope of the study to encompass multiple institutions 
would yield a more comprehensive and generalisable insight into HPC adoption across various 
academic settings.

Authors 
Ndwamai Reginald Mulalo is a PhD candidate in the Department of Human Resource Management and 
Labour Relations at the University of Venda, Thohoyandou, South Africa. His research interests focus 
on high-performance computing systems, organisational behaviour, and human resource management 
practices. Ndwamai has contributed to studies exploring the intersection of technology and management 
in higher education.  
Hlanganipai Ngirande is an Associate Professor in the Department of Human Resource Management 
and Labour Relations and the Extended Curriculum Programme Head of Department at the University 
of Venda, Thohoyandou, South Africa. He has an extensive publication record in organisational 
behaviour, employee engagement, and workplace innovation. His work has appeared in leading 
academic journals, and he has supervised numerous postgraduate students.

Abstract: Understanding how organisational support, perceived ease of use, and perceived usefulness influence the actual use of a High-Performance Computing (HPC) system sheds light on its adoption within a higher education institution. A quantitative approach with a descriptive design was employed, surveying 218 respondents, including Master's and PhD students and academic staff, using stratified and simple random sampling techniques. Data were collected through online self-administered questionnaires and analysed using SPSS version 29.0. The findings revealed strong positive correlations between organisational support, perceived ease of use, perceived usefulness, and actual use of the HPC system, supporting prior research on technology adoption (Davis, 1989; Venkatesh et al., 2003). A moderate positive correlation was found between organisational support and perceived ease of use and perceived usefulness. This suggests that users who feel supported by their institution are more likely to find the system easy to use and valuable. Furthermore, a moderate positive correlation was found between perceived ease of use and perceived usefulness, as well as between perceived ease of use and actual use, indicating that users who find the system simple to use are more likely to adopt it. Additionally, there was a moderate positive correlation between perceived usefulness and actual use, highlighting that users engage more with the system when they recognise its benefits. In conclusion, organisational support and user perceptions are key to successfully implementing and using new technologies.
